title: On the Eve of the Bell-Ringing, a Joint Letter Arrives: 90 Award Winners Question Anthropic's Safety Persona

content_html:
In the early hours of November 20 Beijing time, Anthropic landed on Nasdaq, raising $81.3 billion in its IPO, surpassing SpaceX's $75 billion record to become the largest stock offering in history. It closed up 17.07% on its first day, with a market value of $1.271 trillion. But what rang out earlier than the opening bell was a joint open letter—on the eve of the listing, a statement titled "MisAnthropic Statement" began circulating, aiming directly at the company's "safety persona."

Nobel, Turing, and Fields Awards Rarely Appear Together

The signatory list includes nearly 90 people, spanning several camps that usually hold opposing views: winners of the Nobel Prize, Turing Award, and Fields Medal, AI safety researchers, representatives of the open-source community, and even accelerationists. In their judgment of Anthropic, these people with enormous disagreements stood on the same side for the first time, so the weight is naturally considerable.

Three Allegations Beneath the Safety Slogan

The statement seizes on the disconnect between ideals and practice. First, while Anthropic repeatedly warns that recursively self-improving AI could spin out of control, it continues to push related technologies as a core competitive advantage; second, the company uses its safety image to attract capital and talent, yet is accused of lowering safety standards and lobbying for regulatory rules favorable to itself; third, the signatories question whether it is truly the safety-oriented AI company outsiders believe it to be, and suggest it may instead be using the name of public safety to tighten its grip on technological power in the AI field.

Dramatically, the controversy did not hold back capital's enthusiasm: the bell still rang, and the stock still rose. This rift between "safety" and "business" has now been carried unchanged into the public market, left to every new shareholder.
